title: Barbarian origin; secrecy; shared ethics; handmade gods (chs. 2–5)
english: Celsus next calls the doctrine barbarian from the start — Judaism, from which Christianity hangs — yet grants barbarians can find truths while Greeks better judge and train them; that itself becomes our apology for Greek-trained believers confirming the word. He compares Christian secrecy under death-threat to Socrates’ danger. He sneers that our ethics are common to other philosophers: we answer that without shared notions of right a just judgment of God would be closed. On handmade gods he almost speaks with us: things shaped by base craftsmen are not gods.

title: Power over demons; holding the teaching under threat (chs. 6–9)
english: Celsus hints Christians prevail by demon-names and charms; we answer that expulsion is by the name of Jesus and prayer, not incantation. He almost praises those who hold a good teaching even to death and must not deny it — yet he still mocks the faith. We distinguish the faith taught to the many from the deeper examination for those able to leave all and follow the Word.

title: Faith useful for the many; Celsus’s ‘I know all’ (chs. 10–14)
english: They rail at faith; we confess we teach many to believe even without full inquiry, while opponents do the same in practice without admitting it. Celsus says: if they will answer me as one who cares for all — for I know everything — well; if they say [[do not examine >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 5:21]] and the like, they must still teach what their faith is. We refuse his pose of omniscience and answer from the open Scriptures and the churches’ life.

title: Numenius on nations; world not yet myriad years (chs. 15–20)
english: Numenius the Pythagorean, weighing many doctrines, places among nations that know God as incorporeal the very peoples Celsus scorns. Celsus himself slips into admitting the world is younger and not yet of ten thousand years, saying Greeks count as ancient what floods and conflagrations have erased from memory — testimony against an eternal cosmos of the sort he prefers.

title: Names of God; Jesus’s glory above shame (chs. 21–30)
english: Misplacing the name of God or of the Good is no small danger; Scripture’s names are not idle. Who searches things carefully is struck that Jesus rose in glory above every cause of disgrace and every once-famous name — while human fame rarely holds many honors at once, his name has filled the world after the cross.

title: Virgin birth and [[God with us >> Bible:Matthew 1:23]]; dove at baptism (chs. 31–40)
english: To those who do not know the Hebrew, we still comfort the prophecy that the one at whose birth it is said [[God with us >> Bible:Isaiah 7:14]] [[Matthew 1:23]] is born of a virgin. Celsus next takes from Matthew (and the other Gospels) the dove that came upon the Savior at John’s baptism and tries to dismiss it as fiction — having already mocked the virgin birth.

title: Moses and Jesus; what the prophets foretold (chs. 41–50)
english: In debate with those called wise among the Jews I once asked: of two who visited the human race with wonders beyond nature — Moses and Jesus — whose signs and writings stand? Celsus treats Jesus as if only a judge of the holy and punisher of the unjust were prophesied, ignoring birthplace, passion, resurrection, and mighty works — as if a thousand later claimants were equal.

title: Servant songs vs the people; magi and stronger presence (chs. 51–60)
english: Jewish interlocutors apply the servant prophecies to the whole people in diaspora, struck so that many proselytes come; we read them of the one Christ. To Greeks: magi traffic with demons and achieve nothing divine; when a more divine presence appears, the demonic is put down — as at the magi’s coming to the child.

title: Flee persecution wisely; Celsus’s last abuse — BOOK I CLOSEOUT (chs. 61–71)
english: Jesus taught disciples not to be rash: [[if they persecute you in this city, flee to another >> Bible:Matthew 10:23]], and he himself modeled a steady life that does not court death out of season. Celsus ends in abuse, calling Jesus a god-hated sorcerer; yet properly speaking a human cannot be god-hated, for [[God loves all that is and hates nothing he made >> Bible:Wisdom 11:24]] — prophetic ‘hatred’ language is anthropopathic. BOOK I CLOSEOUT.
